::: {.chapter-lead}
A language model can be described as a system that assigns a probability to a sequence of tokens. In an autoregressive model, this probability is built from successive conditional probabilities: at each position, the model estimates the next token from the prefix already observed. This page makes the mathematical objects behind that idea explicit; the overview does not assume that readers already know them.
:::

::: {.callout-note .learning-outcomes collapse="true" title="Learning outcomes"}
By the end of this page, you will be able to:
- interpret a next-token conditional probability and its notation;
- explain the autoregressive factorization of a sequence probability;
- distinguish the chain rule, the learned model, and the training objective.
:::

## 1. From a text sequence to a token sequence

Assume that text has already been converted by a tokenizer into a sequence of IDs:

$$
x_{1:T}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_T).
$$

Each $x_t$ is an integer belonging to the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$, whose size is $V$. The indices indicate positions in the sequence; they are not numerical values on which arithmetic operations are performed.

Language modeling means constructing a probabilistic model that assigns probabilities to possible sequences. We therefore need to specify what a “sequence probability” means and how context enters the calculation.

## 2. Conditional probability: the next token given its context

For two events $A$ and $B$, with $P(B)>0$, conditional probability is defined as:

$$
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P$B$}.
$$

In a language model, event $B$ represents the prefix already observed and $A$ the next token. We write:

$$
P(x_t\mid x_{<t}),
\qquad x_{<t}=(x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}).
$$

This quantity is the probability assigned to token $x_t$ given the preceding tokens. For a given prefix, the model defines a distribution over the possible tokens in the vocabulary:

$$
\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}P(v\mid x_{<t})=1.
$$

Probabilities depend on context: the same token can receive different probabilities after two different prefixes. It does not have an intrinsic probability independent of its surroundings.

## 3. Factorizing a sequence probability

The probability chain rule gives, for any joint distribution:

$$
P(x_1,\ldots,x_T)
=P$x_1$P(x_2\mid x_1)\cdots
P(x_T\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{T-1}).
$$

Using the notation $x_{<t}$, we obtain:

$$
\boxed{
P(x_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P(x_t\mid x_{<t})
}
$$

This is the autoregressive factorization. It expresses the probability of the sequence as the product of the conditional probabilities of each token, in order.

**Important:** the chain rule is a probabilistic identity, not an assumption specific to Transformers. The autoregressive aspect comes from the order in which the model represents and uses these conditionals: the token at position $t$ is predicted from the prefix, not from future tokens.

For the first token, the prefix is empty. In practice, a beginning-of-sequence token (BOS) may be made explicit, or an equivalent convention may be used.

## 4. What the model learns

A model parameterized by $\theta$ approximates each conditional distribution:

$$
P_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
$$

For an observed sequence, its probability under the model is therefore:

$$
P_\theta(x_{1:T})
=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
$$

The parameters $\theta$ are adjusted to assign high probability to sequences in the training corpus. A standard formulation maximizes the log-likelihood:

$$
\log P_\theta(x_{1:T})
=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
$$

Equivalently, one minimizes the negative log-likelihood, often averaged over tokens and examples. The exact aggregation, masking, and reduction conventions matter when comparing losses; they are detailed in the pages on [likelihood](likelihood.qmd), the [loss function](loss.qmd), and [the mathematical chain of LLM training](mathematical-foundations.qmd).

## 5. A conceptual example

Consider the sequence “The cat sleeps”. After tokenization, suppose it is represented by three tokens $x_1,x_2,x_3$. The model successively assigns:

- a probability to $x_1$ with no prefix (or after a BOS token);
- a probability to $x_2$ given $x_1$;
- a probability to $x_3$ given $x_1,x_2$.

The probability of the entire sequence is the product of these three terms. If one observed token receives a very low probability, the probability of the full product also decreases. This is why training examines probabilities of target tokens, not merely the subjective quality of generated sentences.

## 6. What this formalization does not tell us

- **It does not define the tokenizer.** Text segmentation and vocabulary construction are separate choices ([tokenization strategies](tokenization-strategies.qmd)).
- **It does not specify the architecture.** Several architectures can represent conditional distributions; factorization alone does not imply a Transformer.
- **It does not guarantee truth.** A high probability expresses what the model learned to favor in its data, not factual validation.
- **It does not determine the generation procedure.** Sampling, greedy selection, and other strategies operate after the distribution has been computed ([generation](generation.qmd)).
